meta.title: Morim Foundation
meta.description: Programs for teachers and school coordinators in Israel: intensives, practice with children and real school cases, weekly mentoring, and a stipend for your time.

header.menu_description: Choose a language or get in touch.

hero.title_html: Every year the classroom changes. <mark>The job doesn’t.</mark>
hero.lead: No course can prepare a teacher for every change, least of all the next one. What a teacher can learn is to adapt: to hold on to what the job is for, and rethink the rest. That is what our programs teach.
hero.years_aria: Six years in an Israeli classroom

years.text: COVID. Lessons on Zoom, for months.
The largest wave of aliyah in two decades. New children mid-year, still learning Hebrew.
War. Sirens, shelters, children evacuated from their homes.
A chatbot that can do the homework.
A second school year at war. Children from the north still evacuated, a year on.
Two wars with Iran: twelve days, then six weeks. Schools closed, lessons back online.
Apps engineered to win every minute of a child’s attention.

what_we_do.title_html:
Know the job.
Read the room.
Keep adapting.
what_we_do.lead: Our programs for teachers are built on these three things.

stance.label: the job
stance.title_html: <mark>Curious</mark> children who <mark class="blue">think for themselves</mark> and can <mark class="peach">talk with each other</mark>.
stance.body: That’s what teaching is for, whatever the year brings. Every method we teach is measured against it.

stance.label: the room
stance.body: What walks into the classroom changes from year to year. We name the changes that weigh most on teachers and build the program’s content around them.

stance.label: the habit
stance.body: You try something with real children, go over it with a mentor, and keep what works. The methods we teach are tools for adapting, not a doctrine.

year.title: What we’re working on this year

themes.title: Attention
themes.body: Children are growing up inside an economy engineered to consume their attention. We work on winning it back with the lesson itself: starting from a real question instead of a ready answer, gathering a class without raising your voice, building motivation that doesn’t run on grades.

themes.title: AI
themes.body: Not another “grade homework with ChatGPT” course. Each cohort brainstorms what AI changes in its lessons, drawing on our team’s years in tech and AI education, then tests the three to five best ideas with children in the practice weeks.

year.next_note: will look different. that’s the point.

what_we_do.practice_note: the content changes every year. the structure doesn’t.

how_it_works.heading: How the program works

steps.title: Intensive
steps.body_html: We start with what the job is for and what has changed this year. Then we take practical teaching methods apart, try them on each other, and see what happens.

steps.title: Clubs
steps.body_html: We organize children’s clubs and gather the groups: <mark>over half the program</mark> happens there. For several weeks you lead sessions with real children, where the stakes are low and getting it wrong is allowed.

steps.title: Mentor
steps.body_html: <mark class="blue">Every week, in a small group,</mark> you go over your sessions with a mentor: what went off plan and what to change next time.

steps.title: Your class
steps.body_html: What works, you bring back to your own classroom. That is what the whole program is for.

how_it_works.note: Coordinators go through the same four steps; their practice is real cases from their own schools rather than clubs.

fellowship.title_html: Dear teachers,
intro: if you want a set of techniques that will last until retirement, this isn’t the program for you. If you want to stay good at the job while the world around it keeps changing, it is.
For now, Morim Fellows is for teachers of the later primary and early middle-school years, when many children start to lose interest in learning.
questions: “how do you get a class’s attention without raising your voice?”
“how do you build motivation that doesn’t depend on grades?”
“what is homework for, when a chatbot can do it?”
“how do you start a lesson with a real question?”

intro: Strong teachers need schools where they can do good work and want to stay. That’s why we work with teachers at more than one level: in their own classrooms and in the teams they help lead.
Morim Leaders, our first program for coordinators, is being developed together with rakazim themselves. The first pilot is under way with a closed cohort.

benefits.title: Leading without formal authority
benefits.body:
Rakazim are teachers too. They teach their own classes and help a whole team work better, often without formal authority over the people they lead.
How do you move a team forward when the people in it don’t report to you?

benefits.title: Feedback that actually helps
benefits.body:
How do you give feedback that people can use, support colleagues, and help them grow?
Participants bring real situations from their schools and work through them together with a mentor.

benefits.title: Making room for the work that matters
benefits.body:
How do you distribute the workload across the team and still make time for professional growth — yours and your colleagues’?
The program also covers the practical systems and projects that keep a department running without letting coordination take over the time meant for teaching.

partners.title: For schools and partners
partners.lead: We run our programs with partners: schools that host an extracurricular, organisations that already work with children, and municipalities that want the programs for their own teachers. We are looking for places to practice and people to practice with, not funding.

types.title: Schools
types.body: A fellow runs an after-hours club with your children during the practice weeks. You give a room, a group, and a contact person; we bring the program, the mentor, and the stipend.

types.title: Organisations that work with children
types.body: After-school programs, camps, and youth centres can host practice weeks and gain a trained teacher for a season.

types.title: Municipalities and networks
types.body: Bring the programs to your own teachers and coordinators, cohort by cohort, with practice in your schools.

note.title: The team
note.body: We bring together teacher-development specialists and practicing teachers. We’re also building a circle of experienced Israeli educators and researchers who can tell us when we’re wrong and help us understand the school system from the inside.

questions.a: Practicing teachers in Israel who teach the later years of primary school or the first years of middle school, and who want to keep changing how they teach. If you work with another age group, get in touch anyway and tell us about your experience.

questions.q: Is this an inquiry-based learning program?
questions.a: Inquiry is one of our tools, and the sharpest one we know for building curiosity and intrinsic motivation. But it is slow and it isn’t for every lesson, so we also teach when not to use it.

It is one of this year’s two themes, and we don’t treat it as a tool course. Each cohort works out what AI changes in its own lessons and tests the best ideas with children. Our position: teachers who use AI and teach children to use it, not AI in place of teachers.
Yes. Both teachers and coordinators receive a stipend. The amount and payment arrangements will be provided with the details of each program.

questions.q: Can a school or municipality work with Morim?
questions.a: Yes. We’re looking for schools, networks and municipalities that want our programs for their teachers or coordinators, and for experienced educators who can help us build them. Read about partnering with us.
